input.question: Why is methionine always the "start" codon for proteins?
input.ground_truth: Interestingly, AUG is actually not the only start codon, though it is by far the most popular. [Alternative start codons](_URL_0_) include GUG and UUG. The most interesting thing is that these alternative codons are still translated as Met, regardless of what they typically code for, by using a special start codon tRNA. So, we come back to the same question: why Met? As far as I can tell, nobody really knows.

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: Why is methionine always the "start" codon for proteins?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine you have a set of building blocks to make a special train (that’s like a protein in your body). But you need to know where to start building, right? So, you use a special flag block called "methionine" to say, “Start building here!”

In our body, the instructions for making a train (protein) are written in a code called DNA, and then copied into a message called RNA. This message is made of little pieces called "codons," and each codon tells the body which block (amino acid) to use.

The very first codon in this message is always "AUG," and it always means “put a methionine block here and start building the train.” That’s why methionine is always the first block in almost every protein train your body makes!
